# Key statistics

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# Condition codes in the data (tutor/src/study/studyConfig.js) and their labels here, in the
# same order as the `original` table above.
condition_labels <- c(none = "Control", human = "Human tutor", gpt = "ChatGPT")
n_items <- c(pretest = 3, practice = 5, posttest = 3)

# Key comparison: ChatGPT vs. Control. "gain" = regression of learning gain (post - pre) on
# condition, all three conditions, Control as reference: the ChatGPT coefficient is the
# ChatGPT - Control difference in mean gain, the quantity the original study reported.
# "ancova" = post-test on condition with pre-test as covariate. Set this to the key analysis
# you preregister.
key_method <- "gain"

# Read every event for one phase, including any download-fallback files participants sent in.
read_events <- function(dir) {
  trials <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
  manual <- list.files(file.path(dir, "manual"), pattern = "\\.json$", full.names = TRUE)
  if (length(manual) > 0) {
    trials <- bind_rows(trials, map_dfr(manual, function(f) {
      fromJSON(f, simplifyDataFrame = TRUE) |>
        mutate(across(everything(), ~ if (is.list(.x)) map_chr(.x, ~ toJSON(.x, auto_unbox = TRUE)) else as.character(.x)),
               participant_id = sub("^data-(.*)\\.json$", "\\1", basename(f)), trials_source = "manual")
    }))
  }
  trials |>
    mutate(time = ymd_hms(client_time, quiet = TRUE),
           isCorrect = as.logical(toupper(isCorrect)),
           is_preview = as.logical(toupper(is_preview)))
}

# Load one phase's exported data, build one row per participant, and apply the exclusion rule.
# Returns NULL if that phase has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows
# to skip itself.
#
# The template saves one participant document per page load, so a participant who reloaded has
# two documents. Every event carries a `session_key` (random, made in the participant's browser,
# not an identifier), and participants are rebuilt from it.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  docs   <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
  trials <- read_events(dir)
  errors_path <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()
  
  # Page loads turned away before consent (phones and tablets) have no events.
  n_unsupported <- sum(toupper(docs$device_supported) == "FALSE", na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # Each test item is answered once (no feedback, locked after submitting); use the first
  # submission per item, which is also the first try on each practice item.
  answers <- trials |>
    filter(task == "answer") |>
    arrange(session_key, time) |>
    distinct(session_key, problemID, .keep_all = TRUE)
  
  scores <- answers |>
    filter(study_phase %in% names(n_items)) |>
    group_by(session_key, study_phase) |>
    summarise(items = n_distinct(problemID), score = 100 * mean(isCorrect), .groups = "drop") |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = study_phase, values_from = c(items, score))
  for (col in c(paste0("items_", names(n_items)), paste0("score_", names(n_items)))) {
    if (!col %in% names(scores)) scores[[col]] <- NA_real_
  }
  
  phase_time <- function(task_name, ph) {
    trials |> filter(task == task_name, phase == ph) |>
      group_by(session_key) |> summarise(t = min(time), .groups = "drop")
  }
  timing <- phase_time("phase_start", "pretest") |> rename(t_start = t) |>
    inner_join(phase_time("phase_complete", "posttest") |> rename(t_end = t), by = "session_key") |>
    transmute(session_key, minutes = as.numeric(difftime(t_end, t_start, units = "mins")))
  practice_time <- phase_time("phase_start", "practice") |> rename(t_start = t) |>
    inner_join(phase_time("phase_complete", "practice") |> rename(t_end = t), by = "session_key") |>
    transmute(session_key, practice_minutes = as.numeric(difftime(t_end, t_start, units = "mins")))
  
  # Help used during practice: items where an authored hint was opened, and items where the
  # answer itself (the "bottom-out" hint) was revealed.
  help <- trials |>
    filter(task == "hint_unlock", study_phase == "practice") |>
    group_by(session_key) |>
    summarise(items_authored_help = n_distinct(problemID[hintType != "bottomOut"]),
              items_answer_revealed = n_distinct(problemID[hintType == "bottomOut"]),
              .groups = "drop")
  practice_attempts <- trials |>
    filter(task == "answer", study_phase == "practice") |>
    count(session_key, name = "practice_attempts")
  
  people <- trials |>
    filter(!is.na(session_key)) |>
    group_by(session_key) |>
    summarise(condition_code = first(na.omit(condition)),
              is_preview = any(is_preview %in% TRUE),
              consented = any(task == "consent" & toupper(consented) == "TRUE"),
              declined = any(task == "consent" & toupper(consented) == "FALSE"),
              n_page_loads = n_distinct(participant_id),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(condition = factor(condition_labels[condition_code], levels = condition_labels)) |>
    left_join(scores, by = "session_key") |>
    left_join(timing, by = "session_key") |>
    left_join(practice_time, by = "session_key") |>
    left_join(help, by = "session_key") |>
    left_join(practice_attempts, by = "session_key") |>
    mutate(across(c(items_pretest, items_practice, items_posttest, items_authored_help,
                    items_answer_revealed, practice_attempts), ~ replace_na(.x, 0)),
           pre = score_pretest, post = score_posttest, gain = post - pre)
  
  # Previews are visits without a Prolific id (for example, someone opening the live link).
  n_preview <- sum(people$is_preview & people$consented)
  started  <- people |> filter(consented, !is_preview)
  complete <- started |> filter(items_pretest  >= n_items[["pretest"]],
                                items_practice >= n_items[["practice"]],
                                items_posttest >= n_items[["posttest"]])
  
  # Exclusion rule: replace with the rule  preregistered. Here, as in the original study,
  # participants are analysed if they completed every pre-test, practice and post-test item.
  keep <- complete
  
  list(participants = started, trials = trials, errors = errors, docs = docs,
       complete = complete, keep = keep, answers = answers,
       n_preview = n_preview, n_unsupported = n_unsupported,
       n_declined = sum(people$declined & !people$is_preview))
}

# The key statistic: ChatGPT minus Control, with a 95% CI. NULL until both conditions have at
# least two analysed participants.
#   "gain"   = regression of learning gain on condition (all three conditions, Control as the
#              reference); the ChatGPT coefficient is the ChatGPT - Control difference in mean gain.
#   "ancova" = post-test on condition with pre-test as covariate (ChatGPT and Control only).
key_effect <- function(keep, method = key_method) {
  n_by <- table(keep$condition)
  if (any(n_by[c("Control", "ChatGPT")] < 2)) return(NULL)
  if (method == "gain") {
    d <- keep |> filter(!is.na(condition)) |> droplevels() |>
      mutate(condition = relevel(condition, ref = "Control"))
    fit <- lm(gain ~ condition, data = d)
    if (fit$df.residual < 1) return(NULL)
    ci <- confint(fit)["conditionChatGPT", ]
    co <- summary(fit)$coefficients["conditionChatGPT", ]
    return(tibble(N = nrow(d), estimate = co[["Estimate"]], ci_low = ci[[1]], ci_high = ci[[2]],
                  statistic = co[["t value"]], df = fit$df.residual, p = co[["Pr(>|t|)"]],
                  method = "difference in mean gain (regression on condition)"))
  }
  d <- keep |> filter(condition %in% c("Control", "ChatGPT")) |> droplevels() |>
    mutate(condition = relevel(condition, ref = "Control"))
  fit <- lm(post ~ condition + pre, data = d)
  ci  <- confint(fit)["conditionChatGPT", ]
  co  <- summary(fit)$coefficients["conditionChatGPT", ]
  tibble(N = nrow(d), estimate = co[["Estimate"]], ci_low = ci[[1]], ci_high = ci[[2]],
         statistic = co[["t value"]], df = fit$df.residual, p = co[["Pr(>|t|)"]],
         method = "ANCOVA-adjusted difference in post-test")
}

# The original study's effect: difference in mean gain, ChatGPT minus Control (Welch interval
# if the SDs of the gains are filled in at the top of this file).
original_effect <- function(orig = original) {
  c0 <- orig |> filter(condition == "Control")
  g  <- orig |> filter(condition == "ChatGPT")
  est <- g$gain - c0$gain
  if (anyNA(c(g$sd_gain, c0$sd_gain))) {
    return(tibble(N = c0$n + g$n, estimate = est, ci_low = NA_real_, ci_high = NA_real_,
                  statistic = NA_real_, df = NA_real_, p = NA_real_, method = "difference in mean gain"))
  }
  se <- sqrt(g$sd_gain^2 / g$n + c0$sd_gain^2 / c0$n)
  df <- se^4 / ((g$sd_gain^2 / g$n)^2 / (g$n - 1) + (c0$sd_gain^2 / c0$n)^2 / (c0$n - 1))
  tibble(N = c0$n + g$n, estimate = est, ci_low = est - qt(0.975, df) * se,
         ci_high = est + qt(0.975, df) * se, statistic = est / se, df = df,
         p = 2 * pt(-abs(est / se), df), method = "difference in mean gain")
}

# Mean gain and 95% CI per condition, in the shape the comparison plot needs.
gain_summary <- function(keep) {
  keep |>
    group_by(condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
    summarise(n = n(), gain_mean = mean(gain),
              se = if (n() > 1) sd(gain) / sqrt(n()) else NA_real_, .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(low = gain_mean - qt(0.975, pmax(n - 1, 1)) * se,
           high = gain_mean + qt(0.975, pmax(n - 1, 1)) * se)
}
original_gain_summary <- function(orig = original) {
  orig |>
    transmute(condition = factor(condition, levels = condition_labels), n, gain_mean = gain,
              se = sd_gain / sqrt(n),
              low = gain_mean - qt(0.975, n - 1) * se, high = gain_mean + qt(0.975, n - 1) * se)
}

# Side-by-side figure: mean learning gain per condition for any number of studies, same axes.
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)), label = sprintf("n = %d", n))
  fills <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.6)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = condition, y = gain_mean, colour = Study, group = Study)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey80") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), position = dodge, width = 0, linewidth = 0.8,
                  na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_point(position = dodge, size = 3) +
    geom_text(aes(label = label), position = dodge, hjust = -0.3, size = 3, colour = "grey30",
              show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = fills) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Learning gain (post-test minus pre-test, points)", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Effect (ChatGPT − Control)` = "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", Test = "", p = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Effect (ChatGPT − Control)` = sprintf("%.1f points", r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = if (is.na(r$ci_low)) "" else sprintf("[%.1f, %.1f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         Test = if (is.na(r$statistic)) "" else sprintf("t(%.0f) = %.2f", r$df, r$statistic),
         p = if (is.na(r$p)) "" else format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", original_effect()),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) key_effect(phase1$keep)),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) key_effect(phase2$keep))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrlllr",
               caption = sprintf("Key comparison, ChatGPT minus Control, in percentage points. Original: difference in mean learning gain (Table 2; SDs from the authors' shared data), Welch t-test. Replication: %s.",
                                 if (key_method == "ancova") "difference in post-test score adjusted for pre-test score (ANCOVA)" else "difference in mean learning gain, regression of gain on condition (all three conditions, Control as reference)"))
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

The Pardos and Bhandari speaks directly to my research interests examining how different learning experiences can affect both learning and the student learning process. As someone with a background in AI, Education, and psychology, I am interested in the effectiveness of AI-supported learning and whether educational interventions involving AI-generated instructional support can actually improve learning. I am also interested to explore as well the psychological effects that AI assisted learning may have on students. The Pardos and Bhandari paper is relevant because it experimentally compares ChatGPT-generated help, human tutor help, and a control condition. I would like to choose the statistics experiment as it is relevant to my interests as well as the paper claims that the statistics experiment had the clearest contrast: control −7.6%, human +11.1%, ChatGPT +18.8%.

I will replicate the statistics condition of Pardos and Bhandari using their published materials which comes from the *OpenStax Introductory Statistics* website. I would have the three types of help for the participants (1) The ChatGPT 3.5 worked-solution hints deployed in the original study, as published in the authors' open repository. (2) The hints and content written by human tutors (3) The control group which no help is offered. Participants will answer three background questions regarding their age and prior math experience, and then work through a problem set. The participants will conduct a three-item pre-test, then they will go through a practice problem round, then from there they will retake the same three items as a post-test.

Some challenges that I foresee is the, online participants may on their own use AI tools to answer the test items, so having the integrity of the test takers will be very important. The original model used in the paper (GPT 3.5) is no longer available, I would have to use the original hints verbatim instead of regenerating them. This would keep the replication same but also does limit what we can say about the current models out. I also hope that participants will take their time to do the practice (and read through the hints when applicable). The primary analysis will use linear regression (`score_difference ~ condition`) to examine whether learning gains, calculated as post-test minus pre-test scores, differ across experimental conditions.

A possible extension I would like to look into is how current models are able to help learners, potentially compare models in terms of helpfulness of hints to the learner, and perhaps look at a subject outside of mathematics.

## Methods

### Power analysis

The original sample included 23 participants in the ChatGPT condition, 21 in the human-tutor condition, and 22 in the control condition. Mean gains were 18.83, 11.10, and −7.56 percentage points, respectively. The original unadjusted ChatGPT–control difference in gains was 26.39 percentage points. The standard deviations and standardized effect size were calculated from the shared data.

The corresponding gain standard deviations was 28.11 and 33.99 points which yields a standardized mean difference of approximately Cohen’s d = 0.85. A two-sided independent-groups t-test power calculation with α = .05 indicated that 23, 31, and 38 participants per group would be required for 80%, 90%, and 95% power, respectively assuming an effect of this magnitude.

With keeping the class budget in mind, the proposed target recruitment is asample of 23 per group, roughly 69 analysed in total. At that size we would have 80% power for the original effect and about 29% for an effect half its size. A larger target based on the 2.5× original-sample benchmark discussed by [Simonsohn (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797614567341) and [Experimentology, Section 10.4](https://experimentology.io/010-sampling.html), would not be possible due to budget constraints as this would lead to 166 participants in total.

At \$3.33 per participant, compensation for 69 participants is \$305.90, before additional recruitment and applicable Prolific fees.

### Pilot B

In Pilot B, six participants consented to the study (1 Control, 1 Human Tutor, and 4 ChatGPT). Five participants completed all experimental items, while one participant in the ChatGPT condition dropped out partway through the study.

One participant reloaded the study midway through, but their records were successfully merged.

The median time from pretest to posttest was 8.7 minutes for the Control and Human Tutor conditions and 11.5 minutes for the ChatGPT condition, including approximately five minutes of practice.

The pilot also highlighted the importance of restricting Prolific recruitment to desktop users to prevent participants on unsupported devices from entering the study as two additional participants attempted to access the study using a phone/tablet and were prevented from proceeding before consent.

```{r}
#| label: power
if (anyNA(original$sd_gain)) stop("Fill in sd_gain in the original-study chunk before running the power analysis.")

ctrl <- original |> filter(condition == "Control")
gpt  <- original |> filter(condition == "ChatGPT")

# Named orig_diff (not original_effect) so it does not overwrite the original_effect() function
# defined under Key statistics, which later chunks call.
orig_diff <- gpt$gain - ctrl$gain
sd_pooled <- sqrt(((ctrl$n - 1) * ctrl$sd_gain^2 + (gpt$n - 1) * gpt$sd_gain^2) /
                    (ctrl$n + gpt$n - 2))
orig_d <- orig_diff / sd_pooled

power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- power.t.test(delta = orig_diff, sd = sd_pooled,
                    power = pw, sig.level = 0.05)$n
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n_per_group = ceiling(n), n_total = 3 * ceiling(n))
})

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N per condition", "N total (3 conditions)"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Sample needed to detect the original ChatGPT vs. Control difference in gain (%.1f points, d = %.2f), two-sided alpha = .05.",
               orig_diff, orig_d))
```

```{r}
#| label: power-planned
# Planned sample: the 80%-power sample for the original effect, per condition.
n_planned <- 23

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: %.1f points (d = %.2f)", orig_diff, orig_d),
                         sprintf("Half the original: %.1f points (d = %.2f)", orig_diff / 2, orig_d / 2)),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power.t.test(n = n_planned, delta = orig_diff,     sd = sd_pooled, sig.level = 0.05)$power,
    power.t.test(n = n_planned, delta = orig_diff / 2, sd = sd_pooled, sig.level = 0.05)$power),
    accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf(
    "Planned sample: at least %d analysed participants per condition (80%% power for the original effect). Power for the ChatGPT vs. Control gain difference at %d per group, two-sided alpha = .05.",
    n_planned, n_planned))
```

### Planned sample

Participants will be recruited through Prolific. Participants must use a desktop or laptop computer; phones and tablets will be screened out. The study will be advertised as taking 20 minutes, with compensation of \$3.33 equivalent to approximately \$10 per hour.

Random assignment will use a deterministic hash of each participant’s Prolific identifier, mapped to the three conditions. Assignment will remain stable across reloads but will not guarantee equal group sizes.

Recruitment will continue until at least 69 participants meet the inclusion criteria. Stopping decisions will depend on eligibility and completion, not accuracy, effect estimates, or statistical significance. Unequal group sizes will be accepted. No manual condition overrides or condition-specific top-ups will be used.

The primary analysis will include consenting participants who complete every pretest, practice, and posttest item. Pilot A will be collected under a separate experiment identifier and will not be pooled with the main study.

### Materials

The experiment will use the authors’ OATutor platform and published Statistics materials on independent and mutually exclusive events from OpenStax Statistics Section 3.2. OATutor is integrated with the course experiment template for data storage and export. The experiment is available at the [study website](https://psych251.github.io/pardos2024/).

The pretest and posttest contain the same three items. Questions use typed numerical responses or Yes/No choices. Within each part, problem order is randomized and multiple-choice options are shuffled.

The five practice problems provide correctness feedback and allow repeated attempts. Participants must enter the correct answer before advancing. All conditions therefore include an answer-revealing panel that allows participants to continue if they cannot solve a problem independently. Tests provide neither hints nor correctness feedback.

In the ChatGPT condition, help consists of the original study’s stored ChatGPT 3.5 worked solutions, including the final answer. No new hints will be generated. In the human-tutor condition, help consists of sequential instructional hints, culminating in a scaffold question requiring a response from the participant. Thus, these conditions differ in instructional format as well as source, as in the original study. Control participants receive only answer-revealing help.

Three background questions ask about age group, prior statistics coursework, and prior college mathematics. These questions follow the published materials, although the original article describes only the age question. Each includes a “Prefer not to say” option.

### Procedure

Participants will enter through Prolific and then review the consent form. After consenting, they will receive brief background-question instructions and answer the three background questions.

Separate instruction screens will precede the pretest, practice, and posttest. Each screen will ask participants to complete the task independently without AI tools or internet searches.

Participants will complete the three-item pretest, followed by five practice problems with their assigned form of help. During practice, they may open the available help panels but must submit the correct answer before continuing. They will then complete the three-item posttest, read the debriefing, and proceed through the completion and Prolific return flow.

Pilot A sessions took about 5 minutes. This observed duration is less than 15 minutes from the 20-minute advertised allowance.

The experiment will record responses, correctness, timestamps, help use, phase transitions, and departures from the study tab. Records created by reloads will be joined using the session identifier so that resumed sessions are not treated as separate participants.

### Analysis plan

The key analysis of interest is whether participants receiving ChatGPT-generated hints show greater learning gains than participants in the no-hints control condition.

The analysis plan is to look at the pretest and posttest scores will be the percentage of the three test items answered correctly on first submission. Learning gain will equal posttest minus pretest score, expressed in percentage points.

The primary analysis will use a linear regression model (`score_difference ~ condition`) to examine whether learning gains differ across the three experimental conditions. Condition will be treated as a categorical predictor, with the no-hints control group serving as the reference category. The key analysis of interest will be the difference in learning gains between participants receiving ChatGPT-generated hints and those in the control condition. What will be reported is the estimated difference, its 95% confidence interval, and the associated p-value.

As a **secondary analysis**, we will consider if possible, a linear mixed-effects regression model (`score ~ test_stage * condition + (1 + test_stage | participant_id)`) to examine changes in performance from pretest to posttest across conditions. This model accounts for repeated measurements within participants by allowing each participant to have their own intercept and pretest-to-posttest slope. This helps to capture individual differences in baseline performance and change over time. The interaction between test stage and condition will test whether changes in scores differ across experimental conditions.

Following the original study’s completion requirement, we will analyze participants who consented and completed every pretest, practice, and posttest item. Preview visits without a Prolific identifier will be excluded. Records from page reloads will be joined using the session identifier. Pilot sessions will be kept separate from the main sample through their experiment identifier.

Participants are excluded if they did not complete the study, if they do not consent to the study, or if they are not able to complete the study within the time frame.

### Differences from the original study

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Sample | MTurk in the original study period. | Prolific participants in 2026. | Most likely will not matter as participants both recruited online. |
| Subject coverage | 4 mathematics subjects | Statistics only | Limits generalization and prevents examining differences across subjects. |
| Design | Qualtrics evenly presented conditions | Hash-based assignment without manual top-ups | May produce unequal group sizes. |
| Response | click button | Click a button | no |

```{r}
  fit <- lm(gain ~ condition, data = keep |> mutate(condition = relevel(condition, "Control")))
  print(summary(fit))
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test is significant. Compare the replication estimate and its interval with the original: does the interval exclude zero, and does it include the original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original, or a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original effect, are both informative and should be reported as such (Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- original_effect()
rep  <- key_effect(keep)

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N, Measure = method,
              `Difference (ChatGPT − Control)` = sprintf("%.1f points", estimate),
              `95% CI` = ifelse(is.na(ci_low), "", sprintf("[%.1f, %.1f]", ci_low, ci_high)),
              p = ifelse(is.na(p), "", format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: ChatGPT minus Control, in percentage points.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least two analysed participants in both the ChatGPT and Control conditions.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$estimate >= rep$ci_low & orig$estimate <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.1f points. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    orig$estimate))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and your replication side by side.** It is the single most informative thing in a replication report: a reader can see at a glance whether the effect came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in roughly this order of preference:

1.  **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary statistics (means or proportions, with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot them on the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.

2.  **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or it is in an open repository, using exactly the same plotting code as for your own data.

3.  **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is possible. Save a screenshot of it, for example as `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out in columns:

    ```` markdown
    ::: {layout-ncol=2}

    ```{{r}}
    # your replication plot here
    ```
    :::
    ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and error-bar meaning for both panels, label which is which, and cite the source of the original values or figure in the caption. If the original reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

### Exploratory analyses

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Any follow-up analyses (optional). Label them clearly as exploratory: they were not planned, so they generate hypotheses rather than test them.
:::

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-original-tests
#| eval: !expr have_data
# The original paper's analysis, for one subject: Kruskal-Wallis on gains across conditions,
# then Dunn's pairwise tests (reported unadjusted in the paper; Holm-adjusted here as well).
enough_for_ranks <- n_distinct(keep$condition) == 3 && all(table(keep$condition) >= 3)
if (enough_for_ranks) {
  print(kruskal.test(gain ~ condition, data = keep))
  r <- rank(keep$gain); N <- length(r)
  ties <- table(keep$gain); tie_term <- sum(ties^3 - ties) / (12 * (N - 1))
  mean_rank <- tapply(r, keep$condition, mean); n_c <- table(keep$condition)
  pairs <- list(c("Control", "ChatGPT"), c("Control", "Human tutor"), c("Human tutor", "ChatGPT"))
  map_dfr(pairs, function(pr) {
    z <- (mean_rank[[pr[2]]] - mean_rank[[pr[1]]]) /
      sqrt((N * (N + 1) / 12 - tie_term) * (1 / n_c[[pr[1]]] + 1 / n_c[[pr[2]]]))
    tibble(Comparison = paste(pr[2], "vs", pr[1]), z = round(z, 2), p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)))
  }) |>
    mutate(`p (Holm)` = p.adjust(p, "holm"),
           across(c(p, `p (Holm)`), ~ format.pval(.x, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: Dunn's tests on learning gains (the original study's post hoc test). Positive z: the first condition's gains rank higher.")
} else {
  message("Rank-based tests not run yet: they need at least three analysed participants per condition.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-prepost
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Within each condition, pre-test vs. post-test. The original used a Kruskal-Wallis test here;
# the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test respects that each participant contributes both scores.
if (enough_for_ranks) {
  keep |>
    group_by(Condition = condition) |>
    summarise(N = n(),
              `p (Wilcoxon, paired)` = if (any(post != pre)) wilcox.test(post, pre, paired = TRUE, exact = FALSE)$p.value else NA_real_,
              `p (Kruskal-Wallis, as original)` = kruskal.test(list(pre, post))$p.value,
              .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(across(starts_with("p "), ~ format.pval(.x, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: pre-test vs. post-test within each condition.")
}
```

# Phase 2: Extension

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance: choosing your extension

Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas. In brief:

- **By default the extension is a best-practices modification of your Phase 1 experiment.** If your replication did not succeed, it is a **rescue**: address the plausible reasons for the failure. If it did succeed, it is an **upgrade**: make the estimate more precise. Typical changes are better or more reliable measurement, more trials, a within-participant design where that is legitimate, comprehension and manipulation checks, clearer instructions, or a larger or better-targeted sample.
- **If your scientific extension pitch was approved at Milestone 3 and your replication succeeded, propose that instead:** the original conditions rerun unchanged, plus the one added condition or manipulation, with a power analysis for the new comparison.
- On either track you may add exploratory measures **at the end** of the study.
- Every change is listed and tagged by category below; everything else stays identical.

State your track on the line below, and delete the others.
:::

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade / Best-practices rescue / Scientific extension (approved at Milestone 3)

## Rationale

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs. For a rescue: what are the plausible reasons Phase 1 did not reproduce the original result, and how does each change address one of them? For an upgrade: where is the Phase 1 estimate least precise or least trustworthy, and how will the changes improve it? For a scientific extension: what question does the added condition answer, and why does it follow from the original finding?
:::

## Power and sample

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Justify the Phase 2 sample, and **state how you expect the estimate and its precision to compare with Phase 1**. For an upgrade, plan the sample around the confidence interval you want; for a rescue, around the power to detect the original effect, or the smallest effect you would still consider a successful replication; for a scientific extension, around the power to detect the new comparison. Set `phase2_n_per_group` in the code below; the table uses Phase 1's estimate if you have it and the original's otherwise.
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
#| eval: false
phase2_n_per_group <- 150   # planned analysed participants per condition in Phase 2

p1 <- if (have_data) key_effect(phase1$keep)
sd_basis <- if (have_data && nrow(phase1$keep) > 2) {
  phase1$keep |> filter(condition %in% c("Control", "ChatGPT")) |> group_by(condition) |>
    summarise(s = sd(gain)) |> pull(s) |> mean()
} else {
  mean(original$sd_gain[original$condition %in% c("Control", "ChatGPT")])
}
if (is.na(sd_basis)) stop("Need the SD of gains: from Phase 1 data or `sd_gain` in the original-study chunk.")

effects <- c(Original = original_effect()$estimate,
             if (!is.null(p1)) c(`Phase 1` = p1$estimate),
             `Half the original` = original_effect()$estimate / 2)
tibble(`Effect to detect` = sprintf("%s: %.1f points", names(effects), effects),
       `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(map_dbl(effects, ~ power.t.test(
         n = phase2_n_per_group, delta = .x, sd = sd_basis, sig.level = 0.05)$power), accuracy = 1),
       `Expected 95% CI half-width` = sprintf("±%.1f points",
         qt(0.975, 2 * phase2_n_per_group - 2) * sd_basis * sqrt(2 / phase2_n_per_group))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Phase 2 key test (ChatGPT − Control gain) at %d per condition, two-sided alpha = .05, SD of gains = %.1f.",
                                 phase2_n_per_group, sd_basis))
```
